claims.text: The Gang of Eight is a creature of 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) governing COVERT ACTION findings, not special access programs. The parallel narrowing for DoD SAPs is a different provision with a different membership: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) sends waived-SAP information to 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' -- the six units defined in 119(g), not the intelligence committees and not congressional leadership.

By contrast 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(2) writes an eight-person leadership set INTO the mandatory audience for every controlled access program: 'the majority leader of the Senate; the minority leader of the Senate; the Speaker of the House of Representatives; and the minority leader of the House of Representatives,' alongside the intelligence and appropriations committees. Here the eight is a floor added to committee notice, not a substitute for it.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2): 'If the President determines that it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.'

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that not later than 180 days after a statement of reasons for limited access, the President ensure either that all members of the intelligence committees are provided access to the finding or notification, or that a further statement of reasons is submitted to the Gang of Eight.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported under paragraph (1) or (2) at all, requiring only that the President thereafter 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice.'

50 U.S.C. 3091(e): 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.'

The covert action regime contains a mandatory 180-day review of continued limited access; the DoD waived-SAP regime contains no equivalent, so a waived DoD program can remain restricted to a handful of members indefinitely with no statutory event ever forcing reconsideration. Reasoning: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) has no counterpart in 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

connections.note: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) names the four committee leaders and four chamber leaders to whom a finding may be limited; no SAP statute uses that group.

desc: The phrase 'Gang of Eight' has a precise statutory origin that is routinely misapplied to special access programs, and getting it right matters. Under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(1) a presidential finding authorising covert action must be reported in writing to the congressional intelligence committees as soon as possible after approval and before initiation. Paragraph (2) is the exception: 'If the President determines that it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' Four committee leaders plus four chamber leaders: eight. Since the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, paragraph (5)(A) requires a written statement of the reasons for limiting access, and (5)(B) requires that within 180 days either all members of the intelligence committees get access or a further written statement of reasons is submitted. Paragraph (3) preserves the option of no prior notice at all, requiring only that the President 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' afterwards with a statement of reasons. The DoD waived-SAP convention is a different animal that behaves the same way: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) sends waived information to 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees', and DoD Directive 5205.07 (2010) restricted access for waived programs to 'the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees'. The DoD version has no 180-day sunset, no requirement to widen access ever, and no statutory statement-of-reasons requirement beyond the waiver justification itself. On paper, covert action is better supervised than a waived special access program.
